name: Alfred Wood
bio: An out-of-work clerk who lived three weeks in Taylor's one-bed rooms in January 1893 and was sent to Wilde at the Café Royal by Lord Alfred Douglas's telegram from Salisbury; his testimony describes an act of 'the grossest indecency' at 16 Tite Street, and Wilde was convicted on that count. In a suit of clothes Douglas gave him at Oxford he found Wilde's letters to Douglas — the seed of the Allen-Cliburn blackmail affair — and left for America in spring 1893 with £35 from Wilde; back in London by 1894, he took £175 from a £300-£400 extortion worked with Allen on a gentleman caught with Charles Parker. In De Profundis Wilde described blackmail as the 'sole source of income' of 'people like Alfred Wood.'
bio_sources: Wood's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 201-205 (p. 202 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03; rest djvu OCR)
Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 134-135 (djvu OCR)
Verdict on count 13, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 337 (djvu OCR)
Wilde, De Profundis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 761, with the editors' note 'A blackmailer who gave evidence at Wilde's trials' (p. 761 n 1; read at rendered PDF p. 812, 2026-08-03)
bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far; the Letters editors' note gives none. Ages conflict in the record: Wilde on oath called him 'about twenty-three' in January 1893, while Wood testified he 'was not of age when I went to America' later that year. Taylor dated their first meeting earlier than Wood did (May 1892, at Atkins's rooms, vs. Wood's 'about January 1893'). The letter 'To Mr Wood' at Complete Letters p. 483 ([?Summer 1891]) is editorially 'Unidentified' — a literary correspondent, NOT this Alfred Wood (verified at rendered page 2026-08-03). DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED (2026-08-03). Wood's examination-in-chief in Hyde opens 'ALFRED WOOD, examined by Mr. AVORY - I was formerly a clerk. In January, 1893, I was not in any occupation' - no age is asked or given, which is why the age evidence for him stays the two conflicting second-hand figures already recorded above. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web. Additional checks made so far: the Complete Letters General Index carries only 'Wood, Alfred, 761' and the De Profundis passage at printed p. 761 gives no particulars; McKenna's endnotes cite his 1895 witness statement from a private collection, not a public record. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted. He is said in the trial record to have gone to America in 1893, so a US record would be the place to look.
